content: Efforts to implement nutrition programs globally have been enhanced by sharing detailed programmatic information, country-specific adaptations, and lessons learned. This approach provides practical examples of how guidelines are translated into actionable interventions. The Global Database on the Implementation of Nutrition Action (GINA), launched in November 2012, has become a valuable resource for tracking the implementation of various nutrition policies and interventions. Its usage has steadily increased since its inception. This includes information on health determinants, therapeutic adherence, and program performance metrics. Monitoring disparities in accessibility, availability, acceptability, and quality of interventions across different population groups is critical for designing improved public health programs. Indicators for monitoring can be informed by social determinants of health approaches, enabling the identification and resolution of inequities. The WHO guideline on the use of multiple micronutrient powders for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by infants and young children (aged 6–23 months) and children (aged 2–12 years) emphasizes the importance of sound implementation strategies to scale up efforts effectively. Appropriate monitoring requires the collection and organization of suitable data, and ethical considerations for monitoring systems are outlined in the guideline. The development of this guideline followed WHO's evidence-informed procedures, as detailed in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development, established in 2009, oversees the process and includes representatives from various WHO departments. The guideline development group, active during 2013–2014, provided advice on selecting critical outcomes, interpreting evidence, and formulating recommendations. This group included experts from diverse disciplines and regions, ensuring balanced representation. Members were selected through open calls and expert panels, with efforts to include content specialists, methodologists, and stakeholders such as health professionals and ministry representatives. Commercial organization representatives were excluded from the group. Transparency was maintained by publishing the names and biographies of guideline development group members on the WHO website before meetings. An external group of resource experts assisted in evidence assessment and identifying research priorities but did not participate in decision-making. Peer reviewers provided technical feedback on the final draft, focusing on factual accuracy, clarity, and implementation considerations. The guideline's scope was defined using the Population, Intervention, Control, and Outcomes (PICO) format. Key questions and outcomes were identified and ranked during meetings held in 2013 and 2014. Systematic reviews and evidence profiles, prepared using the GRADE approach, informed the recommendations. Decision-making procedures were established at the outset of meetings, with members voting on the strength and direction of recommendations. If consensus was not achieved, further deliberations and voting rounds were conducted. Conflict-of-interest management was a critical component of the guideline development process. All participants submitted declarations of interest, which were reviewed before finalizing group composition. Participants acted in their individual capacities and verbally declared potential conflicts at the start of meetings. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in micronutrient interventions for infants and children. If updates to the guideline are warranted, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the process following WHO's formal procedures.
